topics.title: Encode, Store, Retrieve
topics.short: Every memory goes through three stages: you take it in (encode), you keep it (store), and you pull it back out (retrieve).
topics.trouble: People blame a bad memory when the real problem was the first stage: the fact never got in, because they were only half paying attention.

topics.title: Your Mental Workbench
topics.short: Working memory holds only a few things at once, about four chunks, so new information has to be grouped or practiced to stay.
topics.trouble: Trying to hold a long list in your head at once. Working memory overflows after about four chunks; the rest falls off the bench.

topics.title: Long-Term Memory
topics.short: Long-term memory holds a huge amount for a long time; the hard part is not space but finding things again.
topics.trouble: Worrying that learning more will "fill up" your memory. Long-term memory has no known limit we can reach; new knowledge gives old knowledge more hooks.

topics.title: You Can't Remember What You Didn't Notice
topics.short: Encoding starts with attention: what you only half notice is never stored well.
topics.trouble: Studying with a screen or music with words in the background, then blaming memory when little sticks.

topics.title: Meaning Makes It Stick
topics.short: Facts you understand and connect to what you know are encoded far better than facts you only repeat.
topics.trouble: Repeating a definition over and over without asking what it means or why it is true.

topics.title: Cues: The Way Back In
topics.short: A cue is any hint that leads you back to a memory: a first letter, a place, a picture, a question.
topics.trouble: Deciding a fact is "gone" because it won't come at once. Often it is stored but needs the right cue.

topics.title: The Forgetting Curve
topics.short: Memory fades fastest right after learning and then more slowly; Hermann Ebbinghaus measured this in the 1880s.
topics.trouble: Thinking forgetting means you did something wrong. Forgetting is normal; the question is how to slow it down.

topics.title: Reading a Forgetting-Curve Graph
topics.short: On a forgetting-curve graph, time runs left to right and memory runs up; each review is a jump back to the top.
topics.trouble: Reading the dashed no-review line as the reviewed line, or thinking a jump means you learned something new.

topics.title: Relearning Is Faster
topics.short: Even when you can't recall something, relearning it takes less time than the first learning; Ebbinghaus called this savings.
topics.trouble: Thinking a forgotten lesson was wasted. Some of it is still there, which is why the second time is quicker.

topics.title: Why Spacing Beats Cramming
topics.short: The same study time spread over several days is remembered far longer than the same time crammed into one sitting.
topics.trouble: Cramming feels effective because recall is high the next morning. A week later most of it is gone.

topics.title: The 1-3-7-21 Schedule
topics.short: A simple starter schedule: learn it, then review on day 1, day 3, day 7 and day 21, each time by recalling first.
topics.trouble: Counting "day 3" from the last review instead of from the day you learned it.

topics.title: Pick the Next Review Day
topics.short: Find the next review on the 1-3-7-21 schedule by asking which reviews are done and counting from the learning day.
topics.trouble: Adding 7 to the last review date instead of to the learning date.

topics.title: The Memory-Work Box
topics.short: A box of index cards with tabs, Daily, Odd/Even, the days of the week and 1 to 31, that spaces reviews out on paper.
topics.trouble: Leaving every card on the Daily tab forever. Cards should move back once they are solid, or the daily review grows too long.

topics.title: The Testing Effect
topics.short: Pulling something from memory strengthens it more than reading it again; a quiz is a way to learn, not only a way to check.
topics.trouble: Using quizzes only to find a grade, and studying by rereading.

topics.title: Why Rereading Fools Us
topics.short: Rereading feels productive because the text looks familiar, but familiarity is not the same as being able to recall it.
topics.trouble: Mistaking "that looks familiar" for "I know it."

topics.title: Narration: Tell It Back
topics.short: Narration means closing the book and telling back what you just read or heard, in your own words.
topics.trouble: Asking a child to narrate a long chapter. Start with a short section, a paragraph or a page.

topics.title: Blank-Page Recall
topics.short: Write down everything you remember on a blank page, then check and fill the gaps in a different color.
topics.trouble: Peeking at the notes after a few seconds. Give your memory a real try, a few minutes, before you check.

topics.title: Flashcards Done Well
topics.short: Good flashcards ask a question you must answer from memory, in both directions, and keep coming back until they are solid.
topics.trouble: Flipping the card before you have tried to answer, or dropping a card after getting it right once.

topics.title: What a Chunk Is
topics.short: A chunk is a group of items you treat as one unit; chunking lets a small working memory hold more.
topics.trouble: Making random groups. Chunks help when each group means something, like a year, a word or a pattern.

topics.title: Chunk a Number
topics.short: Long numbers are easier in groups of three or four, best of all when a group is something you know, like a year.
topics.trouble: Leaving a long number as one string, or splitting it into many tiny pieces.

topics.title: Group a List
topics.short: A long list of words is easier when you sort it into a few groups by kind, then recall group by group.
topics.trouble: Memorizing a shopping list in the order it was written, instead of grouping it.

topics.title: How Many Chunks?
topics.short: Count chunks by dividing the items by the chunk size and rounding up, then compare with the four-chunk workbench.
topics.trouble: Forgetting the leftover group when the items don't divide evenly.

topics.title: Picture Plus Words
topics.short: Learning with a picture and words together gives a memory two paths back; it helps every learner.
topics.trouble: Copying a textbook diagram line by line. A simple sketch you can redraw from memory works better.

topics.title: Make It Vivid
topics.short: Memorable images are concrete, exaggerated, moving and a little funny, and they connect to the thing you need to recall.
topics.trouble: Using a plain, still image that could fit anything. A forgettable image is no help.

topics.title: Learning Styles: What the Evidence Says
topics.short: There is no good evidence that teaching to a "visual" or "auditory" learning style helps; pictures plus words help everyone.
topics.trouble: Labeling yourself a "visual learner" and skipping practice that uses words or speaking.

topics.title: Acronyms
topics.short: An acronym takes the first letter of each item and makes a word or name, like HOMES for the Great Lakes.
topics.trouble: Making an acronym for a list you don't understand. The letters are only cues; you still need to know what each one stands for.

topics.title: Acrostic Sentences
topics.short: An acrostic is a sentence whose words start with the same letters as the items, in order.
topics.trouble: Writing a sentence so long or odd that it is harder to remember than the list.

topics.title: Rhymes, Rhythm and Songs
topics.short: Rhythm and rhyme give words a fixed shape, so a missing word stands out; songs are the oldest memory tool of all.
topics.trouble: Singing the song without knowing which part answers the question.

topics.title: The Keyword Method for New Words
topics.short: To learn a new word, find an English word that sounds like it, then picture the two meanings together.
topics.trouble: Choosing a keyword that sounds alike but can't be pictured.

topics.title: The Memory Palace
topics.short: Place each item along a route through a place you know well; walk the route in your head to recall them in order.
topics.trouble: Using a place you don't know well. The route must come to mind without effort.

topics.title: Choose a Route
topics.short: A good route has distinct spots in a fixed order that you can walk without thinking, about 5 to 10 per room or area.
topics.trouble: Choosing spots that look alike, like six identical chairs, so images blur together.

topics.title: Place and Walk
topics.short: To recall, walk the route spot by spot; the spot's number tells you the item's position.
topics.trouble: Trying to recall the items without walking the route, which loses the order.

topics.title: Sleep On It
topics.short: Sleep helps the brain keep what it practiced; review a little before bed and check in the morning.
topics.trouble: Staying up late to cram. Losing sleep weakens the very memories you were trying to build.

topics.title: Mix It Up
topics.short: In review, mixing kinds of problems or subjects feels harder than doing one kind at a time, but it sticks better.
topics.trouble: Judging practice by how smooth it feels. Blocked practice feels easier and fools you.

topics.title: Teach Someone
topics.short: Explaining what you learned to someone else is retrieval practice, and it shows you what you really understand.
topics.trouble: Teaching from the book. Teach from memory, then check the book together.

topics.title: What Fits Which Age
topics.short: Young children do well with songs, chants and picture cards; ages 8 to 11 add chunking, acronyms and a memory box; 12 and up add self-testing and memory palaces.
topics.trouble: Giving a five-year-old a memory palace, or a teenager only songs. Match the tool to the learner.

topics.title: Your First Session
topics.short: Four steps: choose one small thing, encode it with one tool, retrieve it with the book closed, and space it on the calendar.
topics.trouble: Choosing too much for a first session, like a whole chapter.

topics.title: Spot the Weaker Plan
topics.short: Compare two study plans by checking each habit: spaced or crammed, recall or reread, mixed or blocked, rested or tired.
topics.trouble: Picking the plan that sounds harder-working (more hours) instead of the one that uses better habits.

topics.title: Choose the Technique That Fits
topics.short: Match the tool to the material: palaces for order, chunking for numbers, sketches for structure, acronyms for first letters, songs for exact wording, narration for stories.
topics.trouble: Using one favorite trick for everything.

topics.title: Plan a Memory Session
topics.short: Put it all together: what to learn, which tool, how to recall, when to review, plus sleep and mixing.
topics.trouble: Planning the encoding carefully and forgetting to schedule the reviews.
